title: Model games: how strong players defend
outcomes: Reads win-loss counts with their sample sizes and separates the effect of the rating gap from the effect of the gambit
Explains what Bg4 and Bf7 each prevent and how much the engine says Bd5 gives back
Names the Black ideas that held in strong-player games: the king off f7, the bishop beside the king, two defenders on e5, a safe recapture
Finds the move that punishes a white queen defended only by a pawn (Rh5) and avoids the move that allows the rook sacrifice on e6
Explains why a won game is not proof that every move in it was good

steps.caption: White's knight has just captured on f7, giving a knight for one pawn. Black to move. Hold your first guess: in a fast game, would you take it, and how far ahead do you think Black is afterwards? The engine answers later in the lesson.

claims.statement: A white knight stands on f7.
The black king may capture the knight.

steps.prompt: Before any numbers: in 237 games (almost all fast online games) where White tried this sacrifice, who do you think scored more points, Black or White?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The gambit looks unsound, yet strong players still lose to it sometimes. What do the games Black won show about the defence: which moves keep the extra piece safe, and which hand the advantage back? You will read counts with their sample sizes, then study Black wins move by move. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.prompt: Predict first. Of every 100 points at stake in these games, how many did White score? (A win is one point, a draw half a point.)

steps.text: **What the archive holds.** [V] 237 games reached this gambit: a knight sacrifice on f7 after Black played ...h6. Black won 116, White won 105, 16 were drawn: White scored about 48 per 100. Compare that with your guess: were you close?

**Where the games come from.** [V] 229 carry the site tag chess.com, 228 of them in events named Titled Tuesday or 3-0 Thursday (counted by script; time controls not checked). 98 players had White; Volen Dyulgerov supplies 33. This is one fashionable gambit in fast games, not an objective verdict.

steps.prompt: Predict: in games where Black was rated at least 200 points above White, how many points per 100 did White score?

steps.text:
**The rating gap speaks louder.** [V] White's score per 100, by Black's rating minus White's (234 games with both ratings; a gap of exactly 200 counts in the 200+ row on both sides):
Black 200+ above: 26 (n=54)
Black 50 to 199 above: 40 (n=62)
Within 50: 53 (n=39)
White 50 to 199 above: 64 (n=46)
White 200+ above: 71 (n=33)

steps.prompt: Reading that table: what does it say about using "White scored about 48" as proof that the gambit works?

fields.label: My view:
options: Ratings explain most of the result
It proves the gambit is refuted

steps.text: **By the gambiteer's own rating.** [V] White under 2100: 40 (n=62). 2100 to 2199: 45 (n=63). 2200 to 2299: 47 (n=61). 2300 and up: 62 (n=48). The standard rating formula expected White to score about 45 per 100 from these ratings; White scored about 48. [I] A gain of roughly 3 per 100 is the size chance alone can produce in 234 games, so it is not proof of an edge.

steps.prompt: The engine is next. Predict: after Black takes the knight, by how many pawns does the engine (depth 16) rate Black ahead? Give your best guess to one decimal.

Both Black players were far above their opponents, yet they chose different ninth moves. Black to move: which would you choose, and why?

steps.text: **A win is not a verdict on the moves.** [V] At depth 16 the engine rated Black clearly better after the bishop to g4 or the king to g8, only slightly better after the bishop to d5, and worse after the knight took on e5.

[V] From move 10 to 19 of Willy v Dubov the evaluation swung from slightly favouring Black to clearly favouring White, and the 2708-rated player still won. [I] Copy the move the position supports, not the move that happened to win.

steps.prompt: Which statement would you defend to a friend who says "Dubov won, so 9...Bd5 must be fine"?

steps.text: **A hypothesis about the bishop.** [H] On f7 the bishop guards g6 and h5; on d5 it guards neither. [V] In the 23 games where Black put a bishop on d5 between moves 7 and 12, White's bishop reached g6 by move 22 in 11; in the other 214 games, in 27 (13 per 100). That fits the hypothesis, but White may choose g6 for other reasons; the engine, not the pattern, decides.

steps.text: **Who earned each win?** [I] One depth-16 run, not checked by the validator; each side's costliest moves, in pawns (rough). Haug v Xiong: Black's queen recapture on move 16 cost about 4.3; White's h-pawn push on move 17 about 6. Willy v Dubov: Black's moves 9...Bd5, 10...Nxe5 and 12...Nc5 cost about 1.5, 1.3 and 1.9; White's f-pawn push about 1.3. Vassis in April: Black's e-pawn push about 2.4; White's queen to g3 about 6.3. Black wins here follow error counts as much as defensive skill.

steps.prompt: Sort the games. Which would you copy as a defence, and which owe the result to errors?

steps.text: **One way to sort them.** [I] Haug v Xiong: result owed to errors (the queen recapture gave away about four pawns). Willy v Dubov: owed to errors, since three of Black's own moves cost 1.3 to 1.9 pawns each. Vassis in May: copy with care; the bishop idea held up. Nazari: copy with care; the king stepping off f7, the bishop and the knight together covered e5. Your sort may differ if you can say why.

**What to remember.** [I] Four defensive ideas from these games: (1) Kg8 takes the king off f7, where the knight checks arrive, though with the king on f7 Bg4 is just as good (Haug v Xiong); (2) with the king on g8, Bf7 guards g6 and h5, and Bd5 gives back about a pawn and a half (our depth-16 run); (3) count the pieces that watch e5; (4) recapture so a check cannot win time. [H] The g6 and h5 reason is a hypothesis.

steps.prompt: Teach it back.
